headline: Taiwan Defence Minister Wellington Koo says bipartisan US support continues after midterms despite the $14bn arms package stalled
dek: Taiwan Defence Minister Wellington Koo said on Thursday that Taiwan has always enjoyed cross-party US support and Congress will continue to help strengthen Taipei's defence capabilities, when asked about arms sales after the US midterm elections (Democrats won both houses). The second arms…
sources: Taiwan Defence Minister Wellington Koo, on the record at parliament, via Reuters
fault_line: Bargaining chip or betrayal — is holding Taiwan's $14bn package as leverage with Xi smart statecraft, or does it trade an ally's defence for a deal?

sections.what_happened: Taiwan Defence Minister Wellington Koo said on Thursday that Taiwan has always enjoyed cross-party US support and Congress will continue to help strengthen Taipei's defence capabilities, when asked about arms sales after the US midterm elections (Democrats won both houses). The second arms package, worth about $14 billion, has stalled: President Trump last December approved an $11 billion package (the largest ever), but after meeting Chinese President Xi Jinping in May he called the $14bn package a good 'bargaining chip' held in 'abeyance'. In September, four Republican lawmakers urged the administration to release more than $15 billion in stalled national security assistance for Taiwan, including the $14bn package. Taipei officials have acknowledged the package could be pushed into 2027. Trump is expected to meet Xi at least twice more before year-end: at the APEC summit in China this month and the G20 summit in Florida in December.
sections.what_verified: Single declared family (Reuters, T1) carrying Koo's own on-record statement — the minister himself is the primary source. BusinessToday, Q106FM and MixFM relays carry the same Reuters report and add no independent family.
sections.what_disputed: No contradiction found: Koo's reassurance is consistent with the bipartisan record, but it does not resolve the hold — the package remains unapproved, Trump has not committed to a date, and the 'bargaining chip' framing is Trump's own, not Taipei's. The 49-aircraft surge (Nov 3, triaged at 1000-02(d)) shows Beijing's pressure continues regardless.
sections.why_matters: Pocketbook-meets-power Short: '$14 billion of Taiwan's weapons are sitting on Trump's desk as a bargaining chip with Xi — Taipei says Congress will still deliver.' Low priority (demand 2); lead with the $14bn vs $11bn contrast.
